title: Agent Council
markdown:
The Executive (`openexecutive.orchestrator.executive.Executive`) is a single coherent persona that fans out to specialist sub-agents via Anthropic tool use. Each specialist subclasses `openexecutive.agents.base.BaseAgent`, carrying a `name`, `domain`, and `model`, and exposes `analyze(...)`, which wraps the question in user-turn context and calls Claude through the per-call provider.

Routing uses one `consult_specialist` tool, whose input is only `specialist` and `query`. Multiple parallel `tool_use` blocks in a single assistant turn fan out concurrently through `router.route_parallel`, each running its own domain-filtered ChromaDB query before the specialist sees the question. The Executive then synthesizes the returned analyses into one reply.

That tool shares the turn with roughly 58 other client tools, and a smaller model loses it in the crowd — measured on a local 27B model, a strategic sequencing question reached a specialist on 1 of 12 turns. Two guardrails close that gap. A **routing pre-pass** (`ROUTING_PREPASS_ENABLED`, on by default) runs one call before the main turn offering `consult_specialist` and nothing else, dispatches whatever it picks, and replays the decision into the conversation as a tool_use/tool_result pair; with the persona's consulting section alongside it the same question routed on 9-11 of 12 turns across two runs, while an action request still consulted no one in 0-1 of 12. A pre-pass that picks nobody appends nothing, so action turns behave exactly as before.

The pre-pass runs on a 1,024-token budget, so some of what it emits can be cut off mid-arguments. The rule for discarding a pick is deliberately a single test: **a consult carrying no question is dropped**, wherever it sits and whatever the `stop_reason`. Dispatching one bills a specialist call that can only answer generically and files a consult for a turn that reached nobody — the looks-routed-but-isn't failure the pre-pass exists to fix.

Truncation is the usual source of a blank query, but `stop_reason: max_tokens` is not evidence that any particular call was the casualty: a reasoning model routinely finishes a complete consult and then spends the rest of the budget thinking. An earlier version AND-ed the blank-query test with `max_tokens` and “is the last `tool_use`”, which got both directions wrong at once — it discarded a complete final consult, turning the pre-pass into the no-op it exists to prevent, while still dispatching a blank consult that happened to be emitted first. `stop_reason` is now recorded in the log line for diagnosis rather than used as control flow.

Position was not a safe test either, and not for the reason it first appears. On the OpenRouter path the translator appends a synthetic `openrouter_reasoning` block after the tool_use blocks, so a check keyed on the last content *block* misses the tool_use altogether — but it appends that block only when the response carries `reasoning_details`, an OpenRouter response extension. Against a plain local OpenAI-compatible server (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM) there is no trailing block and a `tool_use` **is** the final content block. Neither arrangement is universal, which is exactly why the rule keys on the query instead.

The `specialist` value is also **normalised before dispatch**. Small models truncate and re-case the enum — `cso` arrives as `cs` or `csO`, `cfo` as `cf` — and an unrecognised name used to be answered with a plain "Unknown specialist" string, so a turn could log three consults while reaching nobody. `router.resolve_specialist_name` case-folds and accepts a prefix that matches exactly one registry key; an ambiguous prefix such as `c` is refused rather than guessed, since routing to the wrong executive is worse than not routing, and every unresolved or corrected name lands in the audit log as a `routing_anomaly` row.

Underneath that sits a broader invariant, enforced at the provider boundary: **a `tool_use` block's `input` is always a dict.** Every tool's `input_schema` here is `type: object`, but only Anthropic's API enforces it — an OpenAI-compatible local server returns whatever `json.loads` produced, including `null`, a list or a number. `translator._parse_tool_arguments` is the single door those arguments come through, so it coerces a non-object payload to `{}` (with a warning) rather than letting each of the ~59 tools discover the problem at its first `.get()`, where it would raise out of a fan-out and end the turn. Specialist-name resolution then has only the string case to worry about.

Normalisation happens in `route_parallel`, before the fan-out — not at dispatch. That placement is the point: a truncated `cs` resolved only at dispatch would still reach the right agent, but the domain-filtered retrieval would be asked for specialist `cs`, miss its alias, and silently fall back to *unfiltered* retrieval; the department-memory prefetch would resolve no slug and be skipped; and the consulted-specialist list would be keyed `cs`, which committee reviewer selection and the department sync both discard. Late normalisation would therefore turn a malformed name into a quietly degraded consult, which is worse than the plain error it used to produce.

The conversation context a specialist receives is supplied by the orchestrator, not written by the model: `route_parallel(conversation_context=...)` forwards a rendered context block — a company-profile digest, then the last two exchanges plus the current message — to every specialist in the batch. The digest (`CompanyProfile.to_specialist_block`) carries company identity, financial position, priorities and north star, target customer and pain points, competitive advantages and competitors, mission and leadership — in that order, because the limit downstream (`_TAIL_PROFILE_MAX_CHARS`, 4,300 chars against 3,187–3,440 on the shipped fixtures) drops whole trailing LINES. Order is what makes an over-long profile shed its roster and mission first. Every list field is rendered one entry per line rather than joined, both because trimming then cannot cut through a figure and because both obvious separators occur inside real entries — ", " inside every leadership entry, "; " inside 3 of 8 tandem competitors. The digest is escaped through `session._inert` before it goes out: profile fields are not first-party, since the engagement-intake agent copies text out of uploaded client documents into them. Market context is carried untrimmed, competitor glosses included, because the CSO is told to name the moat the company actually has, the CMO to position against a specific competitive alternative, and the CPO to clarify the customer problem — and because in the shipped fixtures the later list entries are where the legal and operational facts sit. The tail matters because a specialist sees no message history and no company profile: `<conversation_context>` is its entire view of the conversation, so a follow-up like "what would Legal change if we go ahead with the 30% increase?" is unanswerable without it. The current message keeps its head AND tail, because the channels disagree about where extracted attachment text goes — the web route appends it after the typed question, while the Telegram and Discord paths prepend it. Slicing from one end would preserve the question on some channels and destroy it on others. Extracted document text therefore reaches specialists; an attached **image** does not — `build_attachment_output` returns no text for an image, and the context block is a plain string, so an image is visible to the Executive alone. `_build_messages` appends an `<attachment_notice>` on attachment turns telling the model to restate anything it read from an image inside that consult's `query`. Forwarding the vision blocks themselves needs per-specialist-model vision gating and is tracked in issue #19. The tool deliberately does **not** expose a per-call `context` field. It used to, and the model paid to restate the same background once per specialist. On the six-specialist fan-out measured in issue #12 the routing turn emitted 1,724 output tokens and spent 58.7 s generating them on the local backend before the first specialist started, with the six queries near-verbatim restatements of each other. Re-adding the field would reintroduce that cost silently, so the `query` description carries the matching instruction — one or two sentences, name the subject concretely, and do not repeat company background or the full conversation, which the specialist receives automatically as text — but do restate anything read from an attachment, which it does not receive. The MCP server's separately-defined `consult_specialist` tool still takes a `context` argument, because an external agent has no session here for the orchestrator to render one from.

The nine entries in `SPECIALIST_REGISTRY` (`openexecutive.orchestrator.router`):

| Key | Agent | Domain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cso` | `StrategyAgent` | strategy |
| `cfo` | `FinanceAgent` | finance |
| `chro` | `HRAgent` | hr |
| `gc` | `LegalAgent` | legal |
| `coo` | `OperationsAgent` | operations |
| `cmo` | `MarketingAgent` | marketing |
| `cpo` | `ProductAgent` | product |
| `board_comms` | `BoardCommsAgent` | board |
| `triage` | `TriageAgent` | triage |

Models: specialists default to `claude-sonnet-5`; a deep-reasoning tier uses `claude-opus-5` (adaptive thinking); routing/fast classification uses `claude-haiku-4-5`. The Council's **Deep reasoning** toggle is honoured on Claude Opus/Sonnet (direct or via OpenRouter) and on any OpenRouter model whose live catalog entry supports `reasoning` (today all OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek and Grok entries; not Llama) — the request translator turns Anthropic adaptive thinking + effort into OpenRouter's `reasoning` parameter. It is a silent no-op on models that can't reason, and disabled for Haiku, which rejects adaptive thinking. Self-hosted models on the `LOCAL_*` backend drop adaptive thinking entirely; their reasoning is set deployment-wide by `LOCAL_REASONING_EFFORT` (`none` / `low` / `medium` / `high`), sent as the flat OpenAI-format `reasoning_effort` field on every local call — `none` stops a thinking model such as qwen3 from reasoning on every turn, and leaving it unset keeps the server default. With `OPENROUTER_ENABLED`, the Council dropdown's non-Anthropic entries come from OpenRouter's live `/models` catalog (fetched at startup, refreshed in the background, filtered to tool-capable paid text models from an allowlisted vendor set), falling back to a built-in snapshot if the fetch fails. Six Council-only agents are model/prompt-overridable in the UI but NOT callable via `consult_specialist`, because they are deliberately kept out of `SPECIALIST_REGISTRY`: `quality_judge` (committee review), `utility_fast` (gates, titles, decision parsing), `research` (the `executive_research` fan-out), `fixture_generator` (invents demo companies), `engagement_intake` (models a real client from intake material), and `onboarding_interviewer` (interviews a new user about their own company and drafts its profile, people and departments). The last three share one shape — a forced tool call producing a whole company, validated for referential integrity, with a single repair retry — but opposite epistemics: the fixture author invents, the other two extract and leave unstated facts empty rather than guessing.

One more structured-output utility agent sits beside `triage`: `openexecutive.agents.alert_review.AlertReviewAgent` (routing model, one forced `emit_alert_reviews` tool call, never raises). The alert review job hands it a batch of open alerts with evidence and gets back, per alert, a verdict (relevant / changed / resolved / stale), a confidence, the evidence it relied on, a one-line note, why-now, an optional deadline, and a recommended move (none / route / nudge / escalate / draft / suggest_workflow / merge / close) with its parameters. Like `triage`, it never mutates state — `alerts.review.apply_verdict` executes the verdicts deterministically within authority, so the model's job is judgment, not action.

Every specialist *advises* — each returns domain analysis the Executive synthesizes into one voice. None of them act on the company's behalf; the side-effecting tools in the main loop (schedule, people, departments, broadcast, watchlist, workflows) belong to the Executive, not to a specialist.

The Executive can also launch *any* workflow conversationally: `orchestrator.workflow_run_tools` adds `list_workflows` (the launchable catalog with each workflow's inputs) and `run_workflow` (runs a built-in or custom workflow to completion and returns its artifact, checkpointing approval gates as `awaiting_human`). This makes the `/jobs` catalog reachable from chat — see the Workflows section.

The Executive also backs the **Ask OE** panel's form-fill tier via `orchestrator.form_tools.propose_form_values`: when a chat turn arrives with a `<page_context>` block describing a form on the user's screen, the Executive can propose values for it. The proposal is delivered to the UI as a `form_patch` SSE event and placed into the form as highlighted suggestions — the tool never saves or submits anything; the user reviews and saves manually. The tool is **always** in the tool list (tool definitions sit at the top of the cached prompt prefix, so a conditionally-present tool would invalidate the prompt cache whenever panel and non-panel turns alternate); its description restricts usage to turns that carry a form descriptor.
